entries_new.name: FARC's Caguán zone
aka: San Vicente del Caguán safe haven
entries_new.founder: FARC, by grant of President Andrés Pastrana
entries_new.mechanism: A government granted the guerrillas a demilitarised area during peace talks, then took it back by force when talks ended.
entries_new.story:
The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), a Marxist-Leninist guerrilla group fighting since 1964, was handed a 42,000 square kilometre safe haven by President Andrés Pastrana on 7 November 1998, centred on the town of San Vicente del Caguán, as a confidence-building step for peace talks.
In 2001 Human Rights Watch said FARC had abducted and executed civilians in the zone it accused of helping paramilitaries, without legal defence. After an aircraft hijacking, attacks on towns and kidnappings, Pastrana ended the talks on 21 February 2002 and ordered the army to retake the zone.

entries_new.name: Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, 1996 to 2001
entries_new.stopped_by: Northern Alliance and the United States
entries_new.laws: Sharia as read by the Taliban, Hanafi school, plus Mullah Omar's edicts
entries_new.challenge: Northern Alliance; United States after September 2001
entries_new.recognition: Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates, later withdrawn
entries_new.mechanism: A militia conquered most of a country and ran its courts and law from a provincial base.
entries_new.story:
The Taliban, a militia that first appeared near Kandahar in 1994 with a reported 250,000 US dollars from local businessmen, captured Kabul in 1996 and ran the country as an Islamic emirate. By the end of 2000 it held about 90% of Afghanistan; the Northern Alliance held the northeast and kept broad international recognition.
The government applied its reading of Sharia and the edicts of Mullah Omar and held no elections. Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates withdrew recognition after the 11 September attacks, and the emirate fell on 7 December 2001. The group returned to power in 2021.

entries_new.name: Houthi-held Yemen
entries_new.challenge: Saudi-led coalition; internationally recognised Yemeni government
entries_new.mechanism: An armed movement took the capital and the state offices in it, and rules from them without recognition as Yemen's government.
entries_new.story:
The Houthis, officially Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi Shia movement from Saada in northern Yemen, backed by Iran. By May 2012 they were reported to control most of Saada, Al Jawf and Hajjah governorates. In late 2014, with help from former president Saleh, they took the capital, and on 6 February 2015 they dissolved parliament and named their Revolutionary Committee the acting authority.
A Saudi-led intervention followed to restore the internationally recognised government. A list of rebel-held areas puts Houthi territory at most of former North Yemen and parts of South Yemen, run through a body called the Supreme Political Council. Several countries designate the group as terrorist.

entries_new.name: Hamas administration in Gaza
entries_new.stopped_by: Gaza peace plan after the Israel-Hamas war
entries_new.mechanism: An elected party took one territory by force from its rival and ran a separate government there under blockade.
entries_new.story:
Hamas, a Palestinian Islamist movement with an armed wing, won a majority in the 2006 Palestinian legislative election. In June 2007 it defeated its rival Fatah in fighting in Gaza and from then on governed the Gaza Strip separately from the Palestinian Authority, while being pushed out of government posts in the West Bank. Israel and Egypt imposed an economic blockade.
Many countries and organisations have criticised its rule for human rights violations. After the war that followed its attack of October 2023, Hamas announced on 6 July 2026 that its civil administration was resigning under the Gaza peace plan. A Wikipedia list still shows it holding parts of the Gaza Strip, as sources were written.

entries_new.name: Al-Shabaab areas of Somalia
entries_new.founder: Youth militia of the Islamic Courts Union
entries_new.challenge: Federal Government of Somalia; African Union forces; Ethiopia; Kenya
entries_new.mechanism: An insurgent group runs tax, court and police departments across rural districts the federal government cannot reach.
entries_new.story:
Al-Shabaab began as a youth militia inside the Islamic Courts Union, an alliance that gave de facto government across much of Somalia until Ethiopia invaded in December 2006. It is al-Qaeda's Somali branch and calls its land the Islamic Wilayat of Somalia, which the federal government rejects.
It holds a broken network of mainly rural areas in the south and centre, with its headquarters listed at Jilib. It runs departments for taxation (Zakat), local administration (Wilayah), Islamic courts (Garsoor), police (Jaysh al-Hisbah) and intelligence. An African Union and Somali government coalition took Mogadishu and much other land from it between 2011 and 2013.

entries_new.name: Boko Haram territory in Borno
entries_new.founder: Mohammed Yusuf; Abubakar Shekau led the territorial period
entries_new.stopped_by: Nigerian army and the 2015 West African offensive
entries_new.mechanism: The group seized towns and declared them part of a caliphate.
entries_new.story:
Boko Haram, a jihadist group from northeastern Nigeria founded by Mohammed Yusuf in 2002, moved from raids to holding land in August 2014, when it overran the border town of Gwoza and its leader Abubakar Shekau announced by video that the town was part of an Islamic caliphate. Bama and other towns followed.
By January 2015 the land it held was estimated at 50,000 square kilometres in and around Borno State, though not the state capital Maiduguri. A regional offensive in 2015 took most of this back, and Nigeria's army recaptured Gwoza on 27 March. Smaller holdings in Borno and Kaduna remain listed.

entries_new.name: Kawthoolei, the Karen National Union territories
entries_new.mechanism: A nationalist army built a network of districts with its own schools and clinics in hill country beyond government reach.
entries_new.story:
Kawthoolei is the name Karen nationalists in Myanmar use for the state they have sought since the late 1940s, and for the land the Karen National Union (KNU) holds. The KNU declared war on the government on 31 January 1949 and in 1953 announced a Kawthoolei Free State and sought UN recognition.
In the 1990s it ran seven districts from Manerplaw with hospitals, clinics and schools in the hills of the east. After a 2010s ceasefire its education, health and welfare agencies overlapped with government ones in Mon State, Bago and Tanintharyi. On 7 January 2026 a splinter group, the Kawthoolei Army, declared a Republic of Kawthoolei.

entries_new.name: Greater Liberia
entries_new.currency: Its own currency, name not given in source
entries_new.challenge: Interim Government of National Unity; rival militias
entries_new.mechanism: A warlord turned his militia's land into a state-like business exporting timber, gold and diamonds, then won the presidency.
entries_new.story:
Greater Liberia, or Taylorland, was the land held by Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia during the First Liberian Civil War. From the border town of Butuo, taken on 24 December 1989, it grew to about 90% of the country at its peak. Taylor made Gbarnga his capital and in 1991 set up a civilian government, the National Patriotic Reconstruction Assembly Government, with a justice system under his control.
The area had its own currency and banks, television and radio, airfields, a deepwater port until 1993, and exports of diamonds, timber and gold. Taylor won the war and was elected president in 1997. In 2012 a UN-backed court gave him 50 years for aiding Sierra Leone's RUF rebels.

sources.t: SBS News: Liberia's Charles Taylor sentenced to 50 years

entries_new.name: RUF diamond areas of Sierra Leone
entries_new.challenge: Government of Sierra Leone; West African force; UN
entries_new.cost: War estimated to have cost about 200,000 lives
entries_new.mechanism: Rebels financed a war by holding diamond fields and selling the stones.
entries_new.story:
The Revolutionary United Front (RUF), a rebel group formed by Foday Sankoh with help from Charles Taylor, fought Sierra Leone's government from 1991. It promised free schooling and a fair share of diamond money. Sankoh instead used diamond revenue to buy arms, and the group focused on guarding the mines it held, using child soldiers among the guards. It became known for cutting off civilians' limbs.
On 5 July 2000 the UN Security Council banned rough diamond imports from Sierra Leone, citing the role of the trade in the war. British and other forces weakened the group by 2001. Senior leaders were convicted of war crimes in February 2009.
entries_new.anchor: Kono diamond country, eastern Sierra Leone
